chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Rafi', from Isma'il ibn Sahl, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) left Medina in the remaining days of Sha'ban, and he would fast. Then the month of Ramadan entered upon him while he was traveling, so he broke his fast. He was asked: 'Do you fast Sha'ban and break your fast in the month of Ramadan?' He said: 'Yes, Sha'ban is up to me; if I will, I fast it, and if I will, I do not. And the month of Ramadan is a divine decree (azm) from Allah, the Exalted and Mighty, to break the fast (for the traveler).'

key_terms.السَّفَرِ: Travel/Journey (a state that affects ritual obligations like fasting and prayer)
key_terms.رَمَضَانَ: Ramadan (the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, month of fasting)
key_terms.شَعْبَانُ: Sha'ban (the eighth month of the Islamic calendar)
key_terms.عَزْمٌ: Decree/Resolution (referring to a divine command or established rule)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a traveler who was fasting in Sha'ban when Ramadan begins?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the flexibility of voluntary fasting in Sha'ban and the binding nature of the obligatory Ramadan fast, even for travelers. This narration underscores the concept of 'azm' (divine decree/obligation) in Shia jurisprudence, clarifying that while one may choose to fast in Sha'ban, the traveler's exemption in Ramadan is a specific divine ruling that must be observed. It highlights the theological weight of Ramadan as a month of divine command rather than mere personal piety.
